headline: North Carolina's Hidden Carbon Store: Scientists Race to Save Peatland

body:
In Belhaven, North Carolina, an ambitious restoration effort is underway to save a 23-square-mile tract of peatland—one of the planet's most powerful carbon stores. For centuries, drainage ditches have siphoned water from thousands of years of accumulated peat, leaving the site exposed to drought and wildfire while releasing catastrophic volumes of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Now, scientists and investors backed by Pantheon Regeneration are working to reverse that damage by restoring the water table, a critical step in locking carbon back underground and preventing further ecological collapse.

The stakes are staggering. Peatlands, though they cover just a fraction of Earth's land surface, store one-third of the planet's carbon—more than all the world's forests combined. Yet that protective role inverts the moment peatlands dry out: damaged peatlands become sources of emissions rather than sinks. Pantheon Regeneration's vision extends far beyond this single site. The organization plans to use carbon credits generated from the restoration project to fund an ambitious goal: preserving a million acres of peatland stretching from Virginia to Florida.

At ground level, Duke University researchers including ecology professor Curt Richardson and research scientist Neal Flanagan are conducting careful soil studies in Belhaven to understand what restoration will require. Their work represents the intersection of climate science and practical conservation—measuring the damage, mapping the path forward, and proving that even severely degraded ecosystems can recover. By refilling the ditches and rewetting the peat, these efforts aim to transform a drying liability into a thriving carbon repository, protecting both climate and habitat in one of America's most ecologically vital regions.
quick_facts: 23-square-mile peatland being restored in Belhaven, North Carolina
Peatlands store one-third of global carbon, more than all forests
Pantheon Regeneration aims to preserve 1 million acres from Virginia to Florida
Drained ditches exposed peat to drought, wildfire, and carbon release
